book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

chapters.file: ch02 - The Red Sox and Philosophy.md
ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch05 - The Red Sox and Philosophy.md

chapters.relation: Red Sox official historian Dick Bresciani traces a New England inheritance of endurance from the 1620 Pilgrims through the 1903 first World Series, the fire sale of stars to the Yankees in the 1920s, and the heartbreaks of 1946, 1967, 1975, 1978 and 1986. He argues that the fan virtues of grit, loyalty and cautious optimism mirror the regional character forged by survival, and reads the 2004 ALCS comeback (Millar's walk, Roberts's steal, Ortiz's 12th-inning homer) as the moment fatalism gave way to faith, vindicated again by the 2007 title. The foreword frames the volume as a book by fans for fans that uses the Red Sox to examine faith, morality and community across the history of ideas.

chapters.file: ch08 - The Red Sox and Philosophy.md
ch09 - From Professor Thom’s to the “Little Professor”.md
chapters.relation: Editor Michael Macomber explains that the book grew from watching Red Sox games at Professor Thom's, a Sox bar in Manhattan's East Village, where exiled fans in Yankee territory fused deep game knowledge with intense passion. He argues that Sox fans display the melding of intellectual and emotional lives that philosophers find so tricky, and pays tribute to Dominic DiMaggio, the 'Little Professor,' whose intelligence (as Ted Williams notes in Halberstam's The Teammates) overcame physical shortcomings. DiMaggio's smart, underrated play is offered as the fitting emblem for a book that examines the Red Sox thoughtfully rather than merely emotionally.

chapters.file: ch10 - I - Root Root Root fort Red Sox.md

chapters.relation: Marcus Giamatti narrates his upbringing as an 'Old School' fan under 'Dame Mutability,' his father's personification of the certainty that the Red Sox would always break New England's heart through Bucky Dent, Mookie Wilson, Calvin Schiraldi and Aaron Boone. He argues that being born a Sox fan is an inescapable duty and lifelong quest whose real payoff is not a pennant but the character, faith and perseverance built by enduring, so that when he lay curled up ready to quit during Game Four of the 2004 ALCS, Millar's walk, Roberts's steal and Mueller's single vindicated the whole method. He ends by vowing to pass this philosophy of survival to his unborn daughter Ophelia in Southern California, applying the one-pitch-at-a-time discipline to acting, music and life.

chapters.file: ch12 - Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony.md
chapters.relation: John McHugh uses his urge to confront Grady Little, who left a spent Pedro Martinez in during Game Seven of the 2003 ALCS, to ask how fans should govern the primal emotions fandom generates. Stoic self-command fails because Epictetus's advice (avoid caring about games entirely, focus only on what you control) would extinguish fandom itself, so McHugh adapts Adam Smith's impartial spectator: the virtuous fan imagines being watched by a sympathetic but emotionally distant fellow fan, settling on a Chicago Cubs fan who gets Bartman the way a Sox fan gets Buckner and Grady. He concludes that we each harbor a team of role-specific inner consciences, and the practical task is harmonizing the Red Sox-fan identity with our other identities rather than suppressing it or being consumed by it.

chapters.file: ch13 - The Authentic Red Sox Fan, or The Importance of Turning off NESN and Finding.md
chapters.relation: Corey McCall asks what makes a 'true' Red Sox fan, contrasting the beer-soaked bleacher loudmouth with one-hundred-year-old honorary batboy Arthur Giddon, and treats the nostalgia and resentment around the 2004 bandwagon as the Enlightenment problem of authenticity in miniature. Through Kant's 'Sapere aude' and the ideal of autonomy, he argues the authentic fan is the critical fan who uses reason about the team (questioning Francona's moves, judging whole careers) instead of losing herself in uncritical devotion, reading Jason Varitek's 2004 muzzle of A-Rod as the moment the team's identity crystallized for fans who wanted to be like him. With the Curse gone, fans are freed from fated suffering but inherit Kant's burden of autonomously choosing how fandom will define them, since circumstances no longer decide.

David Roochnik interlaces a loss diary (his daughter's soccer defeat and the Sox's 1998 playoff elimination on the same Saturday, the 2003 Grady Little collapse that gave him chest pain, the 2004 comeback) to argue that losing is an art that teaches what winning cannot. The loser's 'if only' imagination transforms the past, the 'it was only a game' rationalization forces honest reflection about what matters, and shared doom forges Red Sox Nation into a community in a way no Yankees nation could exist, since victors never need to think. He applies Plato's Symposium doctrine of Eros, that to love X is to lack X as Socrates lacks wisdom, to explain why eighty-six years of championship-lack made fandom meaningful, and closes fearing that winning in 2004 and 2007 made the Sox 'normal,' eroding the art of losing that glued the Nation together.

Bryan Pilkington applies Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel's analysis of moral luck, where factors outside an agent's control change how we evaluate the very same act, to Bill Buckner's Game Six error of 1986, alongside constructed cases of Jon Lester skipping the last page of his scouting sheet and a Fenway Franks truck driver who skips his brake check. Drawing on Nagel on negligence, Williams's notion of agent-regret (only Buckner, not Bob Stanley or Rich Gedman, can feel it), and a standard of reasonable expectation for a veteran first baseman, he concludes Buckner can rightly be blamed for the error and even for losing Game Six, though not for the World Series or for the cruel vilification he received. The chapter thus disciplines the fan's 'if only' blame game: a curse is never a satisfying target of blame, but neither is the situation instead of the person.

chapters.file: ch17 - The End of a Curse.md
chapters.relation: Erin Flynn argues that 'the Red Sox are cursed' was never an explanation: it commits the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy and an appeal to ignorance, and a curse, to explain anything, would have to be a force over and above the ordinary causes of losing, which no evidence ever identified. Borrowing Nelson Goodman's 'grue' paradox and the new riddle of induction, he coins 'blursed' (cursed-and-blessed relative to Dave Roberts's steal on October 17th, 2004) to show that the same 1920 to 2003 evidence supports the rival description just as well, so the evidence itself never favored 'cursed.' Since curses explain and predict nothing, the choice between descriptions is pragmatic and aesthetic: 'blursed' rightly renders the 1986 choke as the very thing that made the 2004 comeback the singular, bliss-producing event it was, so the Sox turn out never to have been cursed at all.

chapters.file: ch18 - Only an Ortiz Can Save Us Heidegger’s Revelation of Being.md
chapters.relation: James Pontuso reads Red Sox history through Heidegger: technology that turns the world into 'standing reserve' breeds the anxious 'everydayness' of the mediocre Pinky Higgins teams, while the run of near-misses from 1967 through Bucky Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986 threw fans into an authentic encounter with tragedy, mortality and the mystery of Being that the Yankees' free-agent 'technology of power' could never teach. Fenway Park, quirky and continuous with the pre-Hitler past, serves as 'home' in Heidegger's homeless age, and the literati's tragic framing of the team (language as the house of Being) made its fate a matter of existential weight rather than mere sport. David Ortiz's 2004 ALCS heroics then function as Heidegger's longed-for revelation of Being, the answer to 'only a god can save us,' after which fans have lived through all three states: everydayness, tragic anxiety, and wonder.

chapters.file: ch19 - Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful.md
chapters.relation: Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.

Patrick Tiernan argues that Fenway fandom is a genuine religion: William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity) map onto memories of Buckner's error and Dave Roberts's steal, and Peter Berger's 'signals of transcendence' structure the rituals of Truck Day, the hopes of spring training, the damnation of Bucky Dent and Johnny Damon, and the humor of 'Cowboy Up.' He roots the Curse of the Bambino in New England's Puritan-Calvinist legacy of persecution and original sin (Frazee's sale of Ruth), then deploys Hume's account of superstition from 'Of Superstition and Enthusiasm' to deflate the exorcism rituals fans actually performed, from a Sox hat on Everest to dredging for Ruth's piano, as post hoc fallacies. Even so, the rituals reveal the human need for religious practice, and Maslow's peak experience renders the 2004 comeback a brush with the sacred, so the Faithful believe because they have to.

Karolina Lewestam and Orla Richardson argue that the Red Sox fan is a moral hero in Kierkegaard's sense: like Abraham in Fear and Trembling, the fan fully accepts that loss is inevitable (the Curse, Aaron Boone, Buckner's grounder) yet refuses the rational course of infinite resignation and keeps believing 'this could be the year.' Where liberal individualism licenses walking away from any loyalty and the modern reflex is to sue luck out of existence, the fan lives at the mercy of fate and thereby enacts Kierkegaard's movement beyond resignation into true faith, the absurd belief against all evidence that Isaac will be spared. Fenway thus becomes the best university for learning to live fully under uncertainty, with Ortiz's 'keep the faith' speech and Schilling's bloody sock as its lessons in perseverance and courage.

Chelsea Harry contends that Red Sox Nation embodies a Confucian rather than Cartesian self: against Descartes's cogito and the egocentric, endorsement-chasing player (A-Rod, the traded Manny), the Sox way treats selfhood as constituted by family, community and mutual sacrifice, from Mike Lowell's hometown discount to Yaz's hospital escape and Schilling's bloody sock. She maps Confucian benevolence (jen) onto Wakefield, Varitek and Ortiz describing how fan love powers their play, filial piety onto the retired numbers honoring franchise elders like Pesky, Doerr and Cronin, and Chung-ying Cheng's 'naturality' onto the fans' claim to be the team's twenty-sixth player, so Johnny Damon's defection reads as the treachery of an ungrateful villager. The 'je ne sais quoi' of team spirit is thus Confucian unity: becoming oneself by subordinating the I to the We.

Joel Cade maps baseball's traditionalist-versus-sabermetric war onto the faith-and-reason debate: Joe Morgan's refusal to even read Moneyball repeats Tertullian's fideism, Ted Williams's Science of Hitting exemplifies Augustine's 'faith seeking understanding,' and Wade Boggs's game-day chicken ritual completes his rational hitting exactly as Aquinas says faith completes reason. Theo Epstein's 2004 front office fused the models under the motto 'understanding justifies faith,' using statistics to discover when supposedly obsolete traditional weapons like the stolen base actually work, which is why the seemingly anti-Moneyball Dave Roberts trade paid off in The Steal against Mariano Rivera in Game Four of the ALCS. The chapter closes with the joke that Augustine, who stole pears, would bless stealing second: reconciling faith and reason is how the Sox reversed the Curse, and maybe how faith- and reason-guided people might reconcile.

Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.

chapters.file: ch27 - The Will to Nothingness, or What Happens when the Red Sox Win.md
chapters.relation: Nolen Gertz runs the Sox-Yankees rivalry through Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals: the Steinbrenner Yankees are masters whose 'good' simply means strong and winning, while Sox fans are slaves whose 'Yankees suck!' is ressentiment's imaginary revenge, intensified into the most spiritual and poisonous hatred by eighty-six years of impotence. The priestly slaves defeated the masters by cleverness rather than force, mirrored when Epstein's sabermetric 'religion' of prospects and projections terrified the Yankees into converting, building a farm system and embracing the slavish virtues they had scorned. The final twist is Nietzsche's will to nothingness: once the masters fell in 2004 the fans' suffering lost its meaning, breeding bandwagon guilt, pink-hat resentment and nihilistic exhaustion, so freedom requires a transvaluation that lets fans simply enjoy watching baseball.

holes.name: Nelson Goodman
holes.what: American philosopher (1906-1998) of the new riddle of induction, worldmaking, and the languages of art.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its entire 'blursed' argument on Goodman's grue paradox, entrenchment, and the claim that descriptions construct multiple worlds.

holes.name: The New Riddle of Induction (grue)
holes.what: Goodman's puzzle that the same evidence confirms 'all emeralds are green' and 'all emeralds are grue,' so induction rests on entrenchment rather than evidence alone.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses grue to coin 'blursed,' showing that the evidence for the Curse equally supports a rival description under which 2004 retroactively reveals the team as blessed.

holes.name: Mysticism (knowledge by mystical intuition)
holes.what: The view that certainty and ultimate reality are grasped by direct intuition that transcends logic and even the law of non-contradiction.
holes.why: Chapter 25's stated thesis is that the Red Sox fan's epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics and philosophy of history are all 'Primitive Mysticism' that just knows and embraces paradox.

holes.name: Nihilism (the will to nothingness)
holes.what: Nietzsche's diagnosis that when the values that made suffering meaningful collapse, the will turns against itself and against existence.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues the 2004 championship removed the suffering that structured Red Sox fandom, producing exactly Nietzsche's will to nothingness among the fans.
